item.title: 20 Different Ways To Say “I Know” and “I Understand”
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

Do you often say “I know” or “I understand” in English?

These expressions are perfectly correct, but native English speakers use lots of other phrases to show that they know something, understand an explanation, or recognize what someone is talking about.

And be careful – some expressions can sound friendly and enthusiastic, while others might sound impatient or even rude!

In this lesson, you’ll learn 20 natural English expressions you can use instead of “I know” and “I understand” – as well as their opposites, “I don’t know” and “I don’t understand.” Some are casual, some are idioms, and some have slightly different meanings depending on the situation.

Different Ways to Say “I Know”

1. I’m aware of that.

This means you already know a particular fact or piece of information. It’s a little more formal than simply saying “I know.”

Example:

- A: “The deadline for submitting the application is Friday.”

- B: “Yes, I’m aware of that. I’m planning to submit mine tomorrow.”

Be careful with your tone of voice! If you say “I’m aware of that” in an annoyed tone, it can sound like you’re irritated that someone is telling you something you already know.

2. I heard about that.

Use this when someone tells you some news, but you’ve already received that information from another source.

Example:

- A: “Did you know they’re opening a new shopping mall downtown?”

- B: “Yeah, I heard about that! Apparently, it’s going to have over 100 stores.”

This expression is especially common when talking about news, recent events, and things that are happening in your community.

3. I’m familiar with that.

This means you have some knowledge or experience of a subject, person, or thing.

- A: “Have you ever used this software?”

- B: “Yes, I’m familiar with it. We used it at my previous company.”

4. I’m well aware.

This is an emphatic way to say you already know something. Depending on your tone of voice, it can sound a little annoyed.

- A: “You still have a lot of work to finish.”

- B: “I’m well aware. I’ve been working on it all morning.”

5. I know it by heart.

This means you’ve memorized something so well that you can repeat it without looking.

- A: “Do you need the address?”

- B: “No, I know it by heart. I’ve been there dozens of times.”

Different Ways to Say “I Understand”

6. I see.

This is one of the simplest and most common ways to show that you understand what someone is explaining.

Example:

- A: “We can’t start construction until we get the necessary permits.”

- B: “I see. So we’ll have to wait a few more weeks.”

You can also say “Oh, I see!” when you suddenly understand something that wasn’t clear before.

7. Got it! / Gotcha

This is a short, informal way to say you understand instructions or information.

Example:

- A: “When you get to the building, take the elevator to the third floor and turn right.”

- B: “Got it! Thanks!”

You might also hear “I’ve got it” or “Gotcha!” in casual conversation.

“Got it” is especially useful when someone is giving you directions or explaining what you need to do.

8. That makes sense.

Use this expression when you understand the logic or reasoning behind something.

Example:

- A: “We’re moving the meeting to the afternoon because several people are unavailable in the morning.”

- B: “That makes sense. I’ll update my calendar.”

This phrase doesn’t just mean you understand the information – it also suggests that the explanation seems reasonable to you.

9. I get the picture.

This means you understand the general situation, even if you don’t know every detail.

- A: “The supplier was late, two employees called in sick, and then our computer system stopped working…”

- B: “Okay, I get the picture. You’ve had a really stressful day.”

10. I hear you.

This is an informal expression that means you understand someone’s feelings, concerns, or frustrations.

Example:

- A: “I’m exhausted. It feels like there’s never enough time to get everything done.”

- B: “I hear you. You’ve had a lot on your plate lately.”

Notice that “I hear you” doesn’t simply mean you can physically hear the other person’s voice. Instead, it means you’re listening and you understand how they feel.

It’s especially useful when someone is complaining, expressing frustration, or talking about a difficult situation.

Different Ways to Say “I Don’t Know”

Now let’s look at five more interesting ways to say you don’t know something.

11. Beats me!

This is a very casual way to say you have absolutely no idea.

Example:

- A: “Why is the internet so slow today?”

- B: “Beats me! It was working fine this morning.”

“Beats me” is short, informal, and common in everyday conversations. You wouldn’t normally use it in a formal business email.

12. Your guess is as good as mine.

This expression means you don’t know the answer, and the other person has just as much chance of guessing correctly as you do.

Example:

- A: “When do you think they’ll announce the results?”

- B: “Your guess is as good as mine. They haven’t given us a date.”

It’s often used when both people are uncertain about something.

13. No clue / I don’t have a clue.

This is an emphatic way to say you have absolutely no idea.

Example:

- A: “Do you know where I left my keys?”

- B: “I don’t have a clue. Have you checked your jacket pockets?”

A clue is a piece of information that helps you solve a mystery or find an answer.

So if you haven’t got a clue, you don’t have any information that would help you answer the question.

You can also say “I have no clue” or simply “No clue!”

14. Don’t ask me!

This is an informal expression used when you don’t know the answer, often with a slightly amused, surprised, or frustrated tone.

Example:

- A: “Why does the printer keep breaking?”

- B: “Don’t ask me! I can barely get it to work myself.”

Be careful: depending on your tone of voice, “Don’t ask me!” can sound a little rude or impatient.

It’s best used in casual conversations with people you know well.

15. Who knows?

This is a casual, conversational way to say you don’t know the answer, especially when something is uncertain or difficult to predict.

Example:

- A: “Do you think they’ll lower prices next year?”

- B: “Who knows? They might, but I wouldn’t count on it.”

Although it’s phrased as a question, “Who knows?” isn’t usually asking someone to identify a person who knows the answer. It’s simply expressing uncertainty.

You can also say “Who knows!” with a more enthusiastic tone when talking about exciting possibilities:

- “Maybe I’ll get the job. Who knows!”

Different Ways to Say “I Don’t Understand”

Finally, let’s learn five expressions you can use when something is confusing or difficult to understand.

16. I’m not following.

This is a natural, polite way to say you’re having trouble understanding someone’s explanation.

Example:

- A: “First, we multiply the total by the percentage, then subtract that amount from the original number.”

- B: “Sorry, I’m not following. Could you explain that again?”

You can also say “I’m not sure I follow.”

This is especially useful in meetings, classes, and other situations where you want someone to clarify what they’re saying.

17. You’ve lost me.

This means you were following someone’s explanation at first, but then you became confused.

Example:

- A: “So we transfer the data to the second system, which automatically updates the third database…”

- B: “Wait, you’ve lost me. Why do we need three different systems?”

The idea is that you were mentally following the person, but at some point you couldn’t keep up anymore.

It’s a very natural expression when someone is explaining something complicated.

18. I can’t wrap my head around it.

This idiom means something is extremely difficult for you to understand or accept.

Example:

- A: “The company made record profits last year, but now they’re laying off hundreds of employees.”

- B: “I can’t wrap my head around it. That makes no sense.”

You can also use this expression for complicated concepts:

- “I’ve been studying this math problem for an hour, but I still can’t wrap my head around it.”…

item.title: 33 Common English Words With Multiple Meanings
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

Many common English words have several completely different meanings!

For example, the word fine can mean something is good, but it can also mean a penalty you have to pay. And the word charge can mean asking someone for money, putting electricity into a battery, or officially accusing someone of a crime!

This is one of the reasons English vocabulary can be tricky. Even if you know a word, you might not recognize it when it’s used in a different context.

In today’s lesson, you’ll learn 33 common English words with 3 different meanings each – that’s 99 meanings in total! Each meaning comes with an example sentence to help you understand how the word is used in real life.

Everyday Words with Surprising Meanings

These are words you probably already know, but they have some additional meanings that might surprise you!

1. FINE

Meaning 1: Good, acceptable, or satisfactory

- Don’t worry about me. I’m fine.

Meaning 2: Money that must be paid as punishment for breaking a rule or law

- She had to pay a $100 fine for speeding.

Meaning 3: Very thin, small, or delicate

- The artist used a fine brush to paint the tiny details.

2. BREAK

Meaning 1: To damage something so that it stops working or separates into pieces

- Be careful not to break your phone!

Meaning 2: A short period of rest

- Let’s take a 15-minute break before continuing.

Meaning 3: An opportunity, especially one that leads to success

- He got his big break when a famous director offered him a role.

3. SPOT

Meaning 1: A particular place or location

- This is my favorite spot to sit and read.

Meaning 2: A small mark, stain, or area of a different color

- There’s a spot of coffee on your shirt.

Meaning 3: To notice or recognize something

- Can you spot the difference between these two pictures?

4. MISS

Meaning 1: To feel sad because someone is absent

- I really miss my family when I’m traveling.

Meaning 2: To fail to catch or reach something

- I missed the bus and had to wait another 20 minutes.

Meaning 3: To fail to attend or experience something

- I missed yesterday’s meeting because I was sick.

5. PASS

Meaning 1: To successfully complete a test or examination

- She passed her driving test on the first try.

Meaning 2: To give something to another person

- Could you pass me the salt, please?

Meaning 3: To decline an opportunity or offer

- Thanks for inviting me, but I think I’ll pass this time.

6. FIT

Meaning 1: To be the correct size or shape

- These jeans don’t fit me anymore.

Meaning 2: Healthy and physically strong

- My grandfather is still very fit at the age of 80.

Meaning 3: A sudden period of strong emotion or uncontrolled behavior

- The child threw a fit when his parents said he couldn’t have any candy.

7. SOUND

Meaning 1: Something you hear; a noise

- I heard a strange sound coming from the kitchen.

Meaning 2: To seem or appear a certain way based on what you hear

- That sounds like a great idea!

Meaning 3: Reliable, sensible, or based on good judgment

- My father always gives me sound advice.

8. MATTER

Meaning 1: To be important

- It doesn’t matter what other people think.

Meaning 2: A subject, situation, or problem

- We need to discuss an important matter before the meeting ends.

Meaning 3: Physical substance

- Everything around us is made of matter.

9. POINT

Meaning 1: An idea or argument expressed in a discussion

- You made a good point about the cost of the project.

Meaning 2: The purpose or reason for doing something

- What’s the point of buying a new phone if your old one still works?

Meaning 3: To indicate a person, place, or thing with your finger

- She pointed to the building across the street.

10. CASE

Meaning 1: A particular situation or example

- In this case, I think we should make an exception.

Meaning 2: A legal matter investigated or decided by a court

- The lawyer has been working on this case for months.

Meaning 3: A container used to protect or carry something

- I bought a protective case for my new laptop.

11. CHECK

Meaning 1: To examine something to make sure it’s correct or working properly

- Please check your answers before submitting the test.

Meaning 2: The bill at a restaurant (American English)

- Could we have the check, please?

Meaning 3: A written order instructing a bank to pay money from someone’s account

- She wrote a check to pay the rent.

Common Verbs with Multiple Uses

These everyday verbs are extremely useful because they can express many different actions and ideas depending on the context.

12. RUN

Meaning 1: To move quickly on foot

- I run three miles every morning before work.

Meaning 2: To manage or operate a business or organization

- She runs a small business from her home.

Meaning 3: To function or operate (a machine or system)

- My computer is running much faster since I installed the update.

13. SET

Meaning 1: To put something in a particular place or position

- She set her bag on the floor and sat down.

Meaning 2: To establish or decide something, such as a date, goal, or rule

- We’ve set a deadline for completing the project.

Meaning 3: A group or collection of similar or related things

- My parents gave us a new set of dishes for our wedding.

14. DRAW

Meaning 1: To create a picture using a pencil, pen, or other tool

- My daughter loves to draw animals.

Meaning 2: To attract attention or interest

- The unusual advertisement drew a lot of attention.

Meaning 3: To finish a competition with equal scores

- The two teams drew 2–2.

15. COVER

Meaning 1: To put something over another thing

- Cover the pot and let the soup cook for 20 minutes.

Meaning 2: To include or discuss a particular subject

- Today’s lesson covers 33 common English words.

Meaning 3: To pay for something

- Don’t worry about dinner tonight. I’ll cover the bill.

16. PICK

Meaning 1: To choose or select something

- You can pick whichever restaurant you like.

Meaning 2: To collect fruit, flowers, or vegetables from where they grow

- We went to a farm to pick strawberries.

Meaning 3: To remove something using your fingers or a pointed object

- She carefully picked a piece of glass out of her shoe.

17. HOLD

Meaning 1: To carry or keep something in your hands

- Could you hold my bag for a minute?

Meaning 2: To organize or conduct an event or meeting

- The company will hold its annual conference in June.

Meaning 3: To remain true, valid, or effective

- The same rule holds for everyone, regardless of their position.

18. DROP

Meaning 1: To accidentally let something fall

- I dropped my phone on the sidewalk.

Meaning 2: To decrease or become lower

- Temperatures are expected to drop below freezing tonight.

Meaning 3: To stop doing or participating in something

- He decided to drop the course because he didn’t have enough time.

19. RAISE

Meaning 1: To lift or move something to a higher position

- Please raise your hand if you have a question.

Meaning 2: To increase an amount, price, or level

- The company plans to raise its prices next month.

Meaning 3: To take care of a child as they grow up

- She was raised by her grandparents.

20. TURN

Meaning 1: To move something around a central point or change direction

- Turn the handle to open the door.

Meaning 2: To become or change into a different state

- The leaves turn yellow and orange in the fall.

Meaning 3: An opportunity to do something in a sequence

- It’s your turn to choose a movie.

21. SERVE

Meaning 1: To provide food or drinks

- The restaurant serves breakfast until 11 AM.

Meaning 2: To perform a role, duty, or official position

- She served on the school board for five years.

Meaning 3: To be useful for a particular purpose

- The spare bedroom also serves as my home office.

22. BACK

Meaning 1: The rear part of something

- There’s a small garden at the back of the house.

Meaning 2: To support or agree with someone

- I think it’s a great idea, and I’ll back you all the way.

Meaning 3: To provide financial support for a project or business

- Several investors agreed to back the new company.

Words Used in Work, News, and Formal Contexts…

item.title: What Makes Notre-Dame Cathedral a Masterpiece of Gothic Architecture
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

Most of us remember where we were when we heard that Notre-Dame had burned down. And even upon learning that the most famous of all French cathedrals had been badly damaged rather than completely destroyed, it still felt as if something irreplaceable had been lost. It made no difference whether we’d actually been to the place, as I hadn’t at the time. When I did finally make it to Paris four years later, Notre-Dame’s restoration was still underway, and construction walls prevented anyone from seeing much of anything at ground level, let alone entering. Yet crowds still gathered to take pictures in the square outside, apparently finding that proximity to such a civilizational landmark was enough, even in its partially ruined and inaccessible state.

Even without a chance to step inside, experiencing Notre-Dame’s surroundings on the Île de la Cité, as well as the greater urban context of Paris, certainly deepens one’s understanding of the beauty of the cathedral itself. So does visiting other, less widely known examples of the form, as shown by architecture-and-history YouTuber Manuel Bravo in his new video above.

Ordinary tourists in Paris may make a beeline for Notre-Dame, but they’re hardly likely to find their way out to the other medieval cathedrals in Saint-Denis, north of the city, much less all the way out in Laon. Though glorious in their own way, they’re perhaps even more valuable in providing the context of Gothic church architecture in which Notre-Dame made such a mark.

As Bravo explains it, Notre-Dame’s façade represents “the moment in which Gothic façade achieves its most balanced synthesis. The experiments and innovations of Saint-Denis and Laon are absorbed, disciplined, and unified into a composition in which no element appears arbitrary or independent from the whole.” Among its most influential appreciators was Victor Hugo, in whose time much of Paris’ Gothic architecture was being demolished. His romantic evocations of the medieval built environment in Notre-Dame de Paris (in English, The Hunchback of Notre-Dame) helped save the much deteriorated titular structure, which received an ambitious renovation under Eugène Viollet-le-Duc between 1844 and 1864. That project went beyond period accuracy, adding such non-original details as the gallery of chimeras perched high enough to remain visible during the latest restoration work. Visitors today may notice that the interior doesn’t look exactly like it used to, but some will appreciate that even a monument like Notre-Dame must change with the centuries.

item.title: The Amazing Inventions of Ancient Greece: From Plato’s Alarm Clock to Ancient Flamethrowers
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

“It’s a sunny morning in ancient Greece. Students have started gathering in the Academy, but their famous teacher Plato is nowhere to be seen.” The great philosopher has, it seems, “overslept and missed his own lecture.” The sun and the sound of early-rising animals may have failed Plato that day, as the story goes, but never would he let it happen again — at least after he got the mechanism worked out for the first alarm clock in history. Its design involves a series of containers linked by pipes through which water flows at a steady speed all night long. When the water accumulates in the penultimate, sealed vessel, air is pushed out through the flute embedded in its wall, producing something like birdsong.

Plato’s water alarm clock is just one of the pieces of advanced ancient Greek technology explained in the new video above from Lost in Time, a YouTube channel whose look at ancient Roman technology we posted here on Open Culture last year.

Most of the others were invented for less gentle purposes: we have a nasty-looking flamethrower on wheels meant to breach stone fortresses; a “machine gun” able to fire arrows much more rapidly than any bowman; a nine-story-tall proto-tank fully stocked with catapults and soldiers ready to swarm a city; and a gigantic claw, designed by no less a mind than Archimedes, able to grab and overturn invading warships. Yet as formidable as they sound, evidence of just how all these machines of war worked — and just how well they functioned in actual battle — remains scarce.

Much clearer are records of the Diolkos, recently mentioned here when we featured the megaprojects that even ancient Rome couldn’t pull off. Among those endeavors was a canal across the Isthmus of Corinth, which would save ships having to take the long way around the Peloponnesian peninsula. Or rather, it would save them having to be dragged by a couple hundred slaves over the Diolkos, a paved trackway built in the sixth century BC. Using ramps and winches, ships could be shifted onto a wheeled cart that ran in grooves the whole way, making the whole system a precursor of the railroad, or perhaps an inverted ancestor of the ferry still used to transport railway cars across the Strait of Messina. Like the Romans, the Greeks also considered digging a canal, but to do so might have violated the intentions of Zeus, a better excuse not to build infrastructure than some of those we hear in the twenty-first century.
